agr-facility-structure-vegetables.title: Distinguishing fruit vegetables grown in protected structures
agr-facility-structure-vegetables.objective: Identify the plant families and parts used in tomatoes, strawberries and cucumbers, and distinguish their cultivation and fruit-setting characteristics.

paragraphTitles.agr-facility-structure-vegetables-p1: Separate plant family from the part eaten
paragraphTitles.agr-facility-structure-vegetables-p5: Cucumbers are used as young fruit

paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-vegetables-p1: Vegetables grown in protected structures may all be classed as fruit vegetables while belonging to different plant families. Tomatoes belong to Solanaceae, strawberries to Rosaceae and cucumbers to Cucurbitaceae. Keep classification by use as a fruit vegetable separate from classification by plant family.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-vegetables-p2: When growing tomatoes, consider their need for strong light. Simply putting them inside a structure does not establish that the light conditions are adequate. Consider the crop’s characteristics together with conditions inside the structure.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-vegetables-p3: Tomatoes have several cropping schedules that together support cultivation throughout the year. “Year-round” does not mean that a single plant continuously yields the same quantity. Read it as a combination of cultivation schedules for different times of year.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-vegetables-p4: Strawberries are vegetables whose fruit is used, but vegetative propagation is important when explaining how seedlings are multiplied. Classification of the part harvested and the method of producing new plants are different classification items.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-vegetables-p5: Cucumbers are used while the fruit is still young, before it fully matures. Do not confuse the source’s description of young fruit with harvesting after the seeds have fully matured.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-vegetables-p6: Cucumbers have separate male and female flowers, but they can develop fruit without pollination or fertilization. Consider the separation of flowers separately from whether pollination is necessarily required for fruit to set.

agr-facility-structure-vegetables.activity: Make three columns for each crop: plant family, part used and characteristic discussed in the lesson. Keep these explanatory items separate, rather than assuming that differences in family alone determine cultivation temperatures or management methods.

agr-facility-structure-strawberry.title: Strawberry daughter plants and raised benches
agr-facility-structure-strawberry.objective: Explain propagation through runners and the working characteristics of raised benches, and distinguish flower-bud differentiation from flowering.

paragraphTitles.agr-facility-structure-strawberry-p3: Daughter plants develop at the ends
paragraphTitles.agr-facility-structure-strawberry-p4: The advantage of a raised growing position
paragraphTitles.agr-facility-structure-strawberry-p5: The stage when flower buds form
paragraphTitles.agr-facility-structure-strawberry-p6: How seedling management relates to forcing

paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-strawberry-p1: The strawberry seedling production discussed in the source uses vegetative propagation: new plants develop from part of a parent plant. The mere presence of visible seeds on the fruit is not a reason to describe the propagation method here as sowing.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-strawberry-p2: Runners extending from the parent plant are an important part to observe for propagation. In addition to observing flower- and fruit-bearing parts, check what grows out from the parent plant.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-strawberry-p3: New plants form at the ends of the runners. Explaining the sequence of parent plant, extending runner and daughter plant at its end makes clear which part is used for propagation.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-strawberry-p4: Raised benches allow work in a standing position. “Raised” refers to the height of the growing position, not to the plants themselves being tall.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-strawberry-p5: Flower-bud differentiation is the stage when a bud’s development shifts toward becoming a flower bud. It is separate from the opening of a visible flower, so do not confuse advancing flower-bud differentiation with observing flowering itself.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-strawberry-p6: In strawberries, seedling management that advances flower-bud differentiation is linked to forcing cultivation. Organize daughter-plant production for propagation separately from seedling management intended to control when flowers develop, according to their different purposes.

agr-facility-structure-strawberry.activity: Explain the sequence from parent plant to daughter plant in words. Then separately summarize the benefit of raised benches and the purpose of seedling management that advances flower-bud differentiation, checking that working posture and flowering control have not been confused.

agr-facility-structure-flower-calendar.title: Planning flower shipment schedules
agr-facility-structure-flower-calendar.objective: Explain the short-day response of chrysanthemums and the purpose of supplementary lighting, and distinguish scheduling through combinations of cultivars from low-temperature treatment.

paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-flower-calendar-p: Flowers produced in protected structures include cut flowers shipped after their stems are cut, and plants grown and shipped in pots. Check not only the flower’s name but also the form in which the crop is produced for use.
Shipping flowers throughout the year involves combinations of cropping schedules and cultivars. Year-round shipping does not mean that a single cultivar or one plant continues flowering all year.

Autumn chrysanthemums are treated as short-day plants. When considering flowering time, observe the relationship with the lengths of day and night, not just daytime brightness. This does not mean that every chrysanthemum should be managed under the same day-length conditions.
Supplementary lighting of autumn chrysanthemums supplies light at night to delay flowering. Remembering that adding light always brings flowering forward would reverse the purpose of this treatment.

Different groups, including summer, summer–autumn and autumn chrysanthemums, relate to different flowering seasons. Combining these groups and applying supplementary lighting within a crop are separate approaches that support year-round shipments.

Lilies are grown from bulbs, and treatments such as low-temperature treatment are used to adjust shipment schedules. Do not treat day-length control in chrysanthemums and treatment of lily bulbs as the same method.

agr-facility-structure-flower-calendar.activity: Explain autumn-chrysanthemum lighting, combinations of chrysanthemum groups and low-temperature treatment of lily bulbs by separating the crop concerned from the purpose. Do not invent specific lighting hours or treatment temperatures from this lesson.

agr-facility-structure-flower-forms.title: Plant forms and flower arrangements in cut-flower crops
agr-facility-structure-flower-forms.objective: Explain the differences between flowering woody plants, herbaceous perennials and bulb-grown plants, and describe spray-type carnations.

paragraphTitles.agr-facility-structure-flower-forms-p1: Separate the product from the plant form
paragraphTitles.agr-facility-structure-flower-forms-p5: How flowers are borne on carnations
paragraphTitles.agr-facility-structure-flower-forms-p6: Distinguish repeat flowering from flower type

paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-flower-forms-p1: “Cut flower” describes the form in which a product is shipped and used. Cut-flower crops can be flowering woody plants, herbaceous perennials or plants grown from bulbs. Do not learn cut flowers as a single growth form.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-flower-forms-p2: Roses are grown in protected structures as cut flowers from flowering woody plants. Understand both the plant form and the product: a plant with woody characteristics is used for its cut stems and flowers.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-flower-forms-p3: Chrysanthemums are classified as herbaceous perennials, and shoot cuttings are given as a main propagation method. Distinguish harvesting flowers from the work of multiplying plants.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-flower-forms-p4: Lilies are cut-flower crops grown from bulbs. Trumpet lilies, Asiatic hybrids and Oriental hybrids are among the groups. Separate the shared use of bulbs from the differences among these groups.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-flower-forms-p5: Carnations are herbaceous perennial cut-flower crops. Spray types bear multiple flowers on one stem. When describing flower numbers, observe a single stem as the unit of comparison.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-flower-forms-p6: Carnations include standard types as well as spray types. Organize the ability to flower in different seasons separately from types classified by how flowers are borne.

agr-facility-structure-flower-forms.activity: For the four flowers, summarize plant form and the propagation or flower arrangement described in the lesson. When explaining spray types, make clear what is being compared on one stem rather than counting all flowers on an entire plant.

agr-facility-structure-house-types.title: Covering materials and rain shelters
agr-facility-structure-house-types.objective: Compare glasshouses, plastic houses and rain shelters by their covering materials and the area covered.

paragraphTitles.agr-facility-structure-house-types-p4: Do not combine cost and service life into one measure
paragraphTitles.agr-facility-structure-house-types-p5: A structure covered only at the roof

paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-house-types-p1: When examining types of protected structures, first look at the material covering the exterior. The main categories are glasshouses and plastic houses. This classifies structures from a different perspective than roof shape.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-house-types-p2: Glasshouses transmit light well and are durable enough for long use. However, their construction costs are comparatively higher than structures covered with plastic. Consider durability separately from the initial expense.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-house-types-p3: Compared with glass, plastic materials are light and easy to handle. Nevertheless, the name “plastic” does not mean identical durability: distinguish flexible films from rigid materials.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-house-types-p4: Low construction cost and the ability to use the same material for a long time are separate advantages. Compare glass and plastic in separate columns for cost, weight, handling and durability.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-house-types-p5: Rain shelters have film covering the roof. Do not assume that the word “structure” means the sides are completely enclosed; check exactly which areas are covered.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-house-types-p6: Rain shelters are described as preventing rain from falling directly on crops and helping prevent fruit cracking and pest or disease problems. Do not confuse this rain-sheltering mechanism with a guarantee that pests and diseases will never occur.

agr-facility-structure-house-types.activity: Create a comparison sheet with separate entries for covering material, area covered, cost and durability. Check that a structure with only the roof covered has not been incorrectly described as completely enclosed.

agr-facility-structure-roof-types.title: Single-span and multi-span structures and roof shapes
agr-facility-structure-roof-types.objective: Distinguish the arrangement of spans from roof shape, and match the main shape names to observable features.

paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-roof-types-p1: A single-span structure is based on one roof. The source lists ventilation, sunlight and resistance to wind and snow among its characteristics, but the name alone does not establish the actual wind or snow resistance of the structure being used.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-roof-types-p2: Multi-span structures connect several single spans. They offer a spacious interior, easier working conditions and improved heating efficiency, but less light reaches areas near the connections. Check spaciousness and brightness separately.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-roof-types-p3: A gable roof slopes on both sides. Identify the name by examining the roof’s cross-section, separately from whether there is one span or several. Gable roofs occur in both single-span and multi-span structures.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-roof-types-p4: A curved roof has a rounded outline. This name describes roof shape; the rounded outline alone does not establish that covering materials and all necessary weather precautions are the same.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-roof-types-p5: In a three-quarter roof, the two roof surfaces are not equally wide. The presence of slopes on both sides does not mean their widths are equal; distinguish the wider surface from the narrower one.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-roof-types-p6: The Venlo type is a Dutch-style structure characterized by high eaves. Do not equate roof-peak height with eaves height; identify the part whose height is being described.

agr-facility-structure-roof-types.activity: Explain names using the number of spans, roof outline, widths on each side and position of the eaves. Do not infer wind-resistance ratings or safe snow loads from shape names.

agr-facility-structure-outer-covers.title: Strengths and weaknesses of exterior covering materials
agr-facility-structure-outer-covers.objective: Compare glass, agricultural PVC, agricultural PO films and rigid films in terms of light, weight, soiling and durability.

paragraphTitles.agr-facility-structure-outer-covers-p3: Heat retention and weight of agricultural PVC
paragraphTitles.agr-facility-structure-outer-covers-p6: Do not arbitrarily fix replacement intervals

paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-outer-covers-p1: Exterior covering materials cover the outside of a protected structure. Even materials that look equally transparent differ in weight, ease of handling, heat retention and durability. Do not use apparent transparency as the only basis for comparison.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-outer-covers-p2: Sheet glass used for exterior covering transmits light well. Light transmission matters, but it alone cannot determine material costs, handling or management of the whole structure.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-outer-covers-p3: Agricultural PVC film transmits light and retains heat well. However, its weight, stickiness, tendency to collect dirt and susceptibility to tearing require attention. The Level 1 source also warns that burning it produces toxic gas. Recognize this hazard as well as its benefits, and do not independently choose burning as a disposal method.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-outer-covers-p4: Special agricultural polyolefin (PO) films are lighter and less sticky and collect less dirt than agricultural PVC. Even within the film category, agricultural PVC and PO films should not be treated as having the same properties.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-outer-covers-p5: Rigid films, including agricultural fluoropolymer films, are also used for exterior covering. Both sources mention durability of ten years or more, but this lesson uses that statement to explain material characteristics, not to guarantee the same service life for every product.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-outer-covers-p6: Replacement guidelines differ by material. The two sources also give different ranges of years for agricultural PVC. This lesson does not combine them into one number: learn material characteristics separately from deciding when to replace a product.

agr-facility-structure-outer-covers.activity: Compare agricultural PVC and PO films for weight, stickiness and tendency to collect dirt. Check that statements about durability have not been turned into a guarantee fixing one replacement interval for actual products.

agr-facility-structure-inner-covers.title: Interior covers and what passes through them
agr-facility-structure-inner-covers.objective: Compare transparent films, nonwoven fabric and shade cloth for heat retention and the passage of light, moisture and air.

paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-inner-covers-p1: An interior cover is a covering used inside the structure. Even when a film has the same name as an exterior-cover film, distinguish its position and purpose. Interior-cover films are normally thinner than exterior-cover films.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-inner-covers-p2: Transparent films for interior covering include agricultural PVC, PO, polyethylene and EVA films. Their shared transparency does not mean that their heat retention or handling characteristics are identical.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-inner-covers-p3: Agricultural polyethylene film has poorer heat retention than the other flexible films discussed here. When explaining material selection, consider price and transparency separately from resistance to heat loss.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-inner-covers-p4: Nonwoven fabric is used as a heat-retaining curtain. It transmits less light than transparent film but allows water vapor and water to pass through. Lower light transmission does not mean that nothing can pass through it.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-inner-covers-p5: Shade cloth blocks some light while allowing air through. Understand its shading function together with its breathability; do not describe it as functioning like a sealing transparent film.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-inner-covers-p6: When comparing heat-retaining materials, separately consider which of light, water vapor, water and air can pass through. Explain the several properties shown in the lesson rather than linking a material’s name to just one advantage.

agr-facility-structure-inner-covers.activity: Explain how light, moisture and air pass through nonwoven fabric and shade cloth. Check that heat retention, shading and sealing have not been described as the same function.

agr-facility-structure-heating.title: Heating methods and unheated structures
agr-facility-structure-heating.objective: Explain hot-air heating, hot-water heating and unheated structures, without confusing savings on heating fuel with total costs.

paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-heating-p1: Protected structures can be heated using hot air or hot water. Classify how heat is supplied separately from the names of fuels.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-heating-p2: Hot-air heating is described as easy to install and widely used. Ease of installation alone does not show that it is the least expensive or always the most efficient method for every structure.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-heating-p3: The sources describe heaters using electricity, gas and wood pellets as well as heavy oil and kerosene. Do not restrict the term “heating equipment” to equipment that uses only one kind of fuel.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-heating-p4: Solar-heat use and heat pumps are also listed in relation to heating protected structures. Distinguish learning the names of methods from checking the procedures for installing, connecting and operating individual machines.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-heating-p5: Unheated houses do not use heaters and are described as suitable for cold-tolerant crops. Avoiding heating-fuel costs is an advantage, but it does not mean that all cultivation costs become zero.
paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-heating-p6: Even an unheated house may use an additional tunnel cover to improve heat retention at night. Distinguish reducing heat loss from adding heat with a heater, and do not assume that a particular minimum temperature is guaranteed.

agr-facility-structure-heating.activity: Divide a structure’s description into heating method, energy used and measures for retaining heat. When explaining the advantage of an unheated structure, identify exactly which type of cost is avoided.

agr-facility-structure-cover-functions-2.title: Covering functions and their cultivation context
agr-facility-structure-cover-functions-2.objective: Distinguish light diffusion, heat shielding and UV filtering, and explain their effects on pollinating insects and storage conditions as well as their benefits.

paragraphTitles.agr-facility-structure-cover-functions-2: Consider water on the covering too
Storage conditions for agricultural EVA film

paragraphs.agr-facility-structure-cover-functions-2: The Level 2 source lists light diffusion, which distributes light evenly inside the structure, as a criterion for selecting materials. Distinguish the amount of light transmitted from how incoming light spreads.

Water attached to a covering can block light or be associated with disease. Check functions affecting how droplets form as well. A material’s transparency alone does not mean that the effects of water can be ignored.

UV-filtering functions can help suppress pests and diseases, but they can also suppress honeybee activity. Where pollinating insects are used, do not decide that a material is suitable based only on its effect on pests.
Heat shielding is described as limiting infrared radiation that contributes to high temperatures inside a structure. This is a different role from diffusing incoming light or retaining heat at night.

Rigid exterior-cover materials include acrylic sheets and PC sheets. The source identifies impact resistance as a property of PC sheets, but that alone does not mean they withstand hail or impacts of any severity without damage.

Agricultural EVA film is described as collecting little dust and being relatively nonsticky. However, it may fuse together if left folded in a hot place. Check its advantages in use together with the storage conditions to avoid.

agr-facility-structure-cover-functions-2.activity: Imagine a crop using bees for pollination and explain why UV filtering cannot be evaluated only as an advantage. Also explain heat shielding, heat retention and light diffusion in distinct words.

agr-facility-env-ventilation.title: Understanding ventilation by mechanism and sequence
agr-facility-env-ventilation.objective: Distinguish natural and forced ventilation and explain the sequence of checks when temperatures inside a structure become too high.

paragraphTitles.agr-facility-env-ventilation-p1: Heat builds up during the day
paragraphTitles.agr-facility-env-ventilation-p4: Check the interior covering and roof windows

paragraphs.agr-facility-env-ventilation-p1: Even crops grown under a roof can experience excessive air temperatures as daytime sunlight heats the structure. Ventilation adjusts indoor temperature by bringing in outside air.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-ventilation-p2: Natural ventilation exchanges air by opening ventilation windows or part of the covering. Opening a window alone does not prove that ventilation is sufficient; observe changes indoors, recognizing that this method is affected by the weather.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-ventilation-p3: Forced ventilation exchanges air by running ventilation fans. Its use of electricity and the dependence of its effectiveness on fan capacity distinguish it from natural ventilation.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-ventilation-p4: The source describes starting with natural ventilation, opening the interior covering and then the roof windows. Airflow is affected not only by exterior openings but also by coverings inside them.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-ventilation-p5: The sides are opened if temperatures remain high after the interior covering and roof windows have been opened. Rather than opening every window in the same way from the start, relate the openings used to changes in temperature.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-ventilation-p6: If natural ventilation does not bring the temperature down, forced ventilation is considered next. Separately recording the places opened, their sequence and changes in indoor temperature helps explain the roles of windows and fans.

agr-facility-env-ventilation.activity: Arrange cards for the interior covering, roof windows, sides and ventilation fans, and explain the source’s basic ventilation sequence. Distinguish the decision when the temperature remains high from the decision when it has fallen.

agr-facility-env-co2-light.title: Connecting light and carbon dioxide in a closed structure
agr-facility-env-co2-light.objective: Understand the relationship between photosynthesis and carbon dioxide, and explain why a shortage may develop in a structure kept closed during the day.

paragraphTitles.agr-facility-env-co2-light-p2: Read it as a condition for photosynthesis
paragraphTitles.agr-facility-env-co2-light-p3: A closed space during the day
paragraphTitles.agr-facility-env-co2-light-p5: Do not focus only on quantity

paragraphs.agr-facility-env-co2-light-p1: The Japanese term 炭酸ガス is another name for carbon dioxide, 二酸化炭素. Its appearance in an equipment name does not indicate a substance different from the carbon dioxide discussed in photosynthesis.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-co2-light-p2: The source relates light conditions to the role of carbon dioxide. Do not judge growth only by whether equipment is installed; treat carbon dioxide as an environmental factor involved in photosynthesis when light is available.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-co2-light-p3: Carbon dioxide may become insufficient inside a structure kept closed during the day. Good weather outdoors does not necessarily mean that carbon dioxide inside the structure is sufficient.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-co2-light-p4: A carbon-dioxide generator supplements carbon dioxide inside the structure to promote photosynthesis. Explain its purpose separately from that of a ventilation fan, which exchanges air.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-co2-light-p5: The explanation of photosynthesis does not establish a rule that more carbon dioxide improves growth under every condition. Check light conditions together with the situation in which the structure is kept closed.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-co2-light-p6: Record the periods when the structure was closed, light conditions and the presence of supplementation equipment in separate columns. Learning to connect these three items is separate from setting concentrations or operating conditions on actual equipment.

agr-facility-env-co2-light.activity: Consider a structure kept closed during the day and explain the relationships among light, carbon dioxide and supplementation equipment. Do not add numerical concentrations or operating times that are not in the lesson.

agr-facility-env-temperature-reading.title: Reading current, maximum and minimum temperatures separately
agr-facility-env-temperature-reading.objective: Explain the difference between current readings and recorded maximum and minimum values on thermometers used in protected structures.

paragraphTitles.agr-facility-env-temperature-reading-p1: Temperature management suited to the crop
paragraphTitles.agr-facility-env-temperature-reading-p2: Current readings on a liquid-in-glass thermometer

paragraphs.agr-facility-env-temperature-reading-p1: Temperature management considers the growing temperature suitable for the crop. Distinguishing prevention of daytime overheating from warming during cold early mornings or nights makes the purpose of measurement clear.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-temperature-reading-p2: A rod-shaped thermometer containing colored alcohol shows the temperature at that moment. Label the record as current temperature rather than copying it directly into the column for the highest temperature in the past.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-temperature-reading-p3: A maximum–minimum thermometer shows the current temperature as well as the maximum and minimum since the last reset. Without knowing when the recording period began, you cannot assume that they are the day’s maximum and minimum.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-temperature-reading-p4: On digital instruments too, distinguish the current reading from stored maximum and minimum records. Even if only one number is visible, identify which display item it represents before recording it.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-temperature-reading-p5: Read the liquid column with your eyes level with the liquid. The source uses Celsius, expressed in degrees or ℃. It describes reading the bottom of an alcohol meniscus and the top of a mercury meniscus, so match the reading position to the type of liquid.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-temperature-reading-p6: For the U-shaped maximum–minimum thermometer in the source, read the lower end of the maximum indicator on the right and the minimum indicator on the left. Do not transfer this arrangement to every instrument; compare it with the display and instructions of the actual thermometer.

agr-facility-env-temperature-reading.activity: Make four columns: current temperature, maximum temperature, minimum temperature and time of the last reset. Give an example explaining how confusing these different displays could produce an incorrect record.

agr-facility-env-humidity-control.title: Winter humidity and integrated environmental control
agr-facility-env-humidity-control.objective: Explain excessive humidity and condensation in a closed structure, and the idea of managing several environmental factors together.

paragraphTitles.agr-facility-env-humidity-control-p2: Humidity when the structure is closed
paragraphTitles.agr-facility-env-humidity-control-p4: Relate heating to humidity as well

paragraphs.agr-facility-env-humidity-control-p1: Protected cultivation does not simply accept outdoor conditions unchanged; temperature, humidity and other factors are adjusted. Warm, humid conditions can encourage pests and diseases, so retaining heat is not the only objective.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-humidity-control-p2: Humidity tends to rise in a structure kept closed. An air-temperature reading alone does not establish how moist the air is, so examine temperature and humidity as separate items.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-humidity-control-p3: The source notes that excessive humidity is particularly likely on winter nights and may contribute to disease. When condensation is observed, record the observation of droplets separately from the humidity conditions at that time.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-humidity-control-p4: Heating relates not only to raising air temperature but also to dealing with excessive humidity and condensation. The mere fact that a heater is running does not establish that humidity management is complete.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-humidity-control-p5: Integrated environmental control manages factors such as air temperature, humidity, light and carbon dioxide in combination. Distinguish connecting several factors from changing just one condition and considering the job finished.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-humidity-control-p6: Computers can automate ventilation, heating and other management. Pairing the equipment controlled with the environmental factor to be managed prevents the misconception that every device operates for the same purpose.

agr-facility-env-humidity-control.activity: Using a structure kept closed on a winter night as an example, record air temperature, humidity and condensation observations separately. Explain the relationships by linking ventilation and heating equipment to the environmental factors they manage.

agr-facility-env-growth-observation.title: Measuring and comparing seedling growth in protected cultivation
agr-facility-env-growth-observation.objective: Observe plant height, internodes, true leaves and seedling appearance separately, and keep records without deciding a cause from one symptom alone.

paragraphTitles.agr-facility-env-growth-observation-p2: Separate plant height from internode length
paragraphTitles.agr-facility-env-growth-observation-p5: Describe leaf and stem changes precisely

paragraphs.agr-facility-env-growth-observation-p1: Before giving water or fertilizer, observe how the crop is growing. Separate records of plant height, leaf number, internodes and leaf color allow comparisons that do not rely on general visual impressions alone.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-growth-observation-p2: Plant height describes the height of the whole plant. An internode is the distance between adjacent stem nodes, so it is measured at a different location. Explain changes in overall height separately from lengthening of internodes.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-growth-observation-p3: The source’s leaf-number diagram counts true leaves and excludes cotyledons. Do not add every leaflike part; use the same counting criteria before comparing seedlings or previous records.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-growth-observation-p4: Etiolated seedlings show characteristics such as thin stems and long internodes. The aged-seedling diagram instead shows features such as small leaves, dark coloration and hardened cotyledons. Short internodes alone do not establish that a seedling is healthy.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-growth-observation-p5: Observe lesions, feeding damage and yellowing between leaf veins too. The source gives yellowing of lower leaves as an example of nitrogen deficiency and yellowing of new leaves as an example of iron deficiency, but this is not an exercise in determining a cause from one yellow leaf.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-growth-observation-p6: Water shortage, excessive moisture, excess nitrogen and inadequate light also affect appearance. Rather than immediately increasing water or fertilizer based only on wilting or leaf color, check the affected part separately from conditions such as temperature, light and moisture.

agr-facility-env-growth-observation.activity: For two seedlings, separately record plant height, internode length, true-leaf number, leaf color and the presence of lesions or feeding damage. Leave causes that cannot be established from observation alone as items requiring further checking.

agr-facility-env-hydroponic-systems.title: Distinguishing soilless growing media and equipment
agr-facility-env-hydroponic-systems.objective: Explain whether solid growing media are used in nutrient-solution cultivation and describe the roles of the tank, growing bed and pump.

paragraphTitles.agr-facility-env-hydroponic-systems-p4: Roles of the tank and growing bed
paragraphTitles.agr-facility-env-hydroponic-systems-p5: The pump and delivery of solution
paragraphTitles.agr-facility-env-hydroponic-systems-p6: Work saved and equipment still needed

paragraphs.agr-facility-env-hydroponic-systems-p1: Unlike soil cultivation, nutrient-solution cultivation grows crops with nutrients dissolved in water. Do not describe it as growing plants in water alone: the solution contains nutrients.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-hydroponic-systems-p2: Some systems use rockwool, coconut coir, peat moss or gravel as solid media. The presence of solid material around the roots does not by itself place a system in the same category as ordinary soil cultivation.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-hydroponic-systems-p3: Hydroponic and air–water culture systems are listed as methods without solid media. In air–water culture, most roots extend into the air; distinguish methods by where the roots are located.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-hydroponic-systems-p4: The tank that stores nutrient solution is not the same part as the bed where crops grow. When identifying equipment, point out the storage location and growing location separately.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-hydroponic-systems-p5: The pump sends nutrient solution to the growing bed. Systems may recirculate the solution or use a nonrecirculating, run-to-waste arrangement. A pump’s presence alone does not show that the solution is reused.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-hydroponic-systems-p6: The source lists fewer soil-borne disease problems, the ability to omit work such as soil preparation and weeding, and ease of automation as characteristics. However, equipment construction costs are still necessary; crop management and checking equipment do not become unnecessary.

agr-facility-env-hydroponic-systems.activity: Draw the place storing solution, the place growing crops and the device delivering solution, and label them tank, growing bed and pump. Also explain systems with and without solid growing media.

agr-facility-env-nursery-methods.title: Distinguishing nursery methods by their beds and containers
agr-facility-env-nursery-methods.objective: Explain ground-bed, box, pot, paper-pot and cell-tray nursery methods through differences in nursery beds and containers.

paragraphTitles.agr-facility-env-nursery-methods-p6: Connect the name to the container

paragraphs.agr-facility-env-nursery-methods-p1: Ground-bed nursery production establishes a bed for sowing. The source’s unheated bed requires no special materials, while a heated bed warms the bed soil using heating wires or similar means. Separate the use of a nursery bed from whether heat is supplied.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-nursery-methods-p2: Box nursery production uses a seedling box. Contrasting the shared box with separate pots for individual seedlings makes the relationship between equipment and method clear.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-nursery-methods-p3: Pot nursery production uses plastic containers of various sizes. Even though they are all called pots, do not assume that they have identical dimensions; check the actual containers.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-nursery-methods-p4: Paper-pot production sows seeds in paper containers that decompose in soil. Their division into small compartments does not mean they are made of the same material as plastic cell trays.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-nursery-methods-p5: Cell-tray nursery production uses dedicated trays divided into compartments. Cell counts vary according to the vegetable and seedling size; different cell counts do not necessarily provide the same space for each seedling.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-nursery-methods-p6: To distinguish methods, examine whether seedlings use a soil bed, a box, individual pots or compartmented containers. Explain names by structure and material, not merely by the colors in container photographs.

agr-facility-env-nursery-methods.activity: Match the five methods to the characteristics of soil beds, boxes, plastic pots, paper containers and cell trays. Explain them without confusing method names with container names.

agr-facility-env-grafted-seedlings.title: Distinguishing rootstock and scion in grafted seedlings
agr-facility-env-grafted-seedlings.objective: Distinguish the properties sought in rootstocks and scions and connect these with observations of seedling health and etiolation.

paragraphs.agr-facility-env-grafted-seedlings-p1: A grafted seedling is made by joining a scion to a rootstock. Although both names concern the same seedling, the parts have different roles; consider separately what is required of each.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-grafted-seedlings-p2: The sources use varieties or crops resistant to diseases and pests as rootstocks. Do not learn only the name of the harvested variety: include the resistance sought in the rootstock among the seedling’s component characteristics.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-grafted-seedlings-p3: The scion is described as a variety selected for high yield and good quality. Do not reverse the roles of the rootstock, chosen for resistance, and the scion, chosen for characteristics of the harvested product.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-grafted-seedlings-p4: Grafted seedlings are used for eggplants, cucumbers, tomatoes, watermelons and other crops. These examples do not show that every crop uses the same rootstock or that only one grafting method exists.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-grafted-seedlings-p5: Descriptions of good seedlings include short internodes, thick stems and a sturdy appearance. Do not finish selecting a seedling based only on the name “grafted”; also examine how it has grown.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-grafted-seedlings-p6: Excessive moisture, high temperatures and inadequate light are associated with etiolation. Treat learning rootstock–scion combinations and providing an appropriate nursery environment as separate checks; grafting does not eliminate the need for management.

agr-facility-env-grafted-seedlings.activity: Make separate rootstock and scion columns and assign cards for resistance, yield and quality. Add checks of seedling appearance and nursery temperature, light and moisture, then explain the relationships.

agr-facility-env-soil-indicators-2.title: Reading soil-type and pF examples with their conditions
agr-facility-env-soil-indicators-2.objective: Distinguish percentage soil-water content from pF values and explain the Level 2 source’s figures without separating them from soil type and conditions.

paragraphTitles.agr-facility-env-soil-indicators-2-p2: The same percentage in different soil types
paragraphTitles.agr-facility-env-soil-indicators-2-p3: The direction in which values change
paragraphTitles.agr-facility-env-soil-indicators-2-p4: The range stated in the Level 2 text

paragraphs.agr-facility-env-soil-indicators-2-p1: The Level 2 source distinguishes percentage displays on soil-moisture meters from pF displays on tensiometers. The same number need not represent the same scale, so record the display type along with the value.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-soil-indicators-2-p2: In the source’s example at 15% soil-water content, sandy soil is approximately pF 3.2 and Kuroboku soil approximately pF 4.6. Do not judge the two soils to have the same water status from the percentage alone.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-soil-indicators-2-p3: This source explains that pF decreases as the soil contains more water. Do not read a higher pF number as meaning more moisture; distinguish it from the intuitive reading of a percentage.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-soil-indicators-2-p4: The Level 2 text gives 1.8–2.7 as a pF range favorable for growth. Treat this as the source’s statement, and do not transfer it directly to every structure’s automatic irrigation settings without checking the crop, soil and measurement conditions.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-soil-indicators-2-p5: The same text indicates moisture shortage at 3.0 or above, the beginning of wilting around 3.8 and plant death if 4.0 or above persists. Distinguish the stages and the requirement of continued conditions; one value alone does not establish the state of every crop.
paragraphs.agr-facility-env-soil-indicators-2-p6: Excess water is described as reducing soil air and leading to root damage. Do not keep adding water based only on figures for dry conditions: check excessive-moisture conditions too, together with crop observations.

agr-facility-env-soil-indicators-2.activity: Compare the source’s 15% example in three columns for soil type, percentage and pF. Separately organize the Level 2 text’s range and statements about shortage, wilting and persistence, distinguishing these from actual irrigation settings.

agr-facility-env-solution-circulation-2.title: Comparing recirculating and run-to-waste nutrient solutions
agr-facility-env-solution-circulation-2.objective: Explain differences between recirculating and nonrecirculating systems in solution stability, disease spread and effluent treatment.

paragraphTitles.agr-facility-env-solution-circulation-2-: Composition and quantity in a recirculating system
Do not select a system by advantages alone

paragraphs.agr-facility-env-solution-circulation-2-: Recirculating nutrient solution and discharging it after one use involve different handling. The type of medium supporting roots is a different classification from whether the solution is reused.

The Level 2 source explains that continuous circulation stabilizes nutrient-solution composition and quantity and reduces waste-solution treatment. Less waste solution does not mean there is no longer any solution to manage.
The source warns that disease arising in a recirculating system can spread rapidly. Compare the benefit of reusing solution together with precautions concerning disease spread.
Disease spread is described as less extensive in run-to-waste systems than in recirculating systems. This is a comparison with systems returning solution, not a claim that disease never occurs.

Run-to-waste systems require effluent treatment. The source does not specify individual treatment procedures, so do not reinterpret this as permission to discharge directly into waterways; leave it as work requiring further checking.

Make separate comparison columns for stability of composition and quantity, disease spread and effluent treatment. Match the characteristics of each system rather than dividing them into simplistic claims that recirculation is better in every respect or that run-to-waste systems need no concern about disease.

agr-facility-env-solution-circulation-2.activity: Draw one route that returns solution and another that does not, and compare composition and quantity, disease and effluent treatment. Do not add treatment equipment or disinfection conditions absent from the source.

agr-fruit-foundation-life.title: Considering tree age separately from yield
agr-fruit-foundation-life.objective: Explain changes from young to old trees and distinguish tree size from the amount of fruit borne.

paragraphTitles.agr-fruit-foundation-life-p1: The role of the period after planting
paragraphTitles.agr-fruit-foundation-life-p5: Connect the years with tree species

paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-life-p1: Fruit-tree cultivation includes several years of growing the tree rather than aiming only for harvest immediately after planting. Separate the period of building tree size from the period of bearing and harvesting fruit.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-life-p2: The life-cycle diagram shows successive stages of juvenile, young, mature and old trees. These categories describe growth and fruit bearing; they do not mean that the same quantity is harvested from the year of planting onward.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-life-p3: The line for tree size and the line for fruit quantity do not follow the same pattern. Separate records of tree growth from records of how much fruit was borne, avoiding predictions of yield based on size alone.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-life-p4: The diagram shows abundant fruit bearing at maturity, followed by decreases in tree size and fruit quantity in old age. Even a mature tree cannot remain unchanged and produce harvests forever.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-life-p5: The text describes a productive harvesting period of 20–40 years, varying by species. The age scale on the diagram, however, illustrates schematic changes. Do not turn it into a schedule in which every tree starts fruiting and declines at the same age.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-life-p6: When reading an orchard plan, distinguish the period of growing trees, the harvesting period and the period when trees age. Considering changes over several years, not only one year’s harvest work, is characteristic of fruit-tree cultivation.

agr-fruit-foundation-life.activity: Organize a fruit tree’s life into three stages and explain tree size and fruit quantity separately. Also explain why the diagram cannot establish an exact year when harvesting begins.

agr-fruit-foundation-buds.title: Examining branches by locating flower buds
agr-fruit-foundation-buds.objective: Distinguish leaf buds from flower buds and connect differences in flower-bearing branches with pruning decisions.

paragraphTitles.agr-fruit-foundation-buds-p2: This year’s fruit and preparation in the previous year
paragraphTitles.agr-fruit-foundation-buds-p3: Examples using the previous year’s branches
paragraphTitles.agr-fruit-foundation-buds-p5: Pair the location with the species

paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-buds-p1: Buds on a branch do not all have the same role. Distinguishing leaf buds that produce leaves from flower buds associated with flowering is the starting point for deciding whether to retain or cut a branch.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-buds-p2: Many fruit trees form flower buds before the year in which the fruit is harvested. Do not assume that preparation for fruit bearing begins only on the day flowers open; follow the condition of branches and buds from the preceding year too.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-buds-p3: Peaches and cherries are described as forming flower buds on branches that grew in the previous year. Cutting off all young branches as unnecessary could remove flower-bearing parts as well.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-buds-p4: Grapes are shown as a type that flowers on newly growing shoots. Distinguish flowers borne directly on the previous year’s branches from those borne after new shoots grow, rather than applying the same pruning method to every species.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-buds-p5: Satsuma mandarins are described as having both patterns of flower-bearing branches. Bud location affects which branches are retained, so identify the fruit-tree species before reading which branches bear flowers.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-buds-p6: Management listed as supporting flower-bud differentiation includes limiting excessive nitrogen effects, light pruning, avoiding excessive fruit load and keeping soil moisture slightly restrained. Do not turn this into an instruction to cut off nutrients and water regardless of tree condition.

agr-fruit-foundation-buds.activity: Describe the difference between flower-bearing branches in peaches and grapes. Also explain the problem with applying the same pruning without checking flower-bud locations.

agr-fruit-foundation-propagation.title: Propagating fruit trees: rootstocks and scions
agr-fruit-foundation-propagation.objective: Distinguish seed propagation from vegetative propagation and explain the properties sought in rootstocks and scions.

paragraphTitles.agr-fruit-foundation-propagation-p3: What is required of a rootstock
paragraphTitles.agr-fruit-foundation-propagation-p4: What is required of a scion

paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-propagation-p1: Fruit-tree nursery plants can be grown from seeds or from plant parts such as branches. Grafting and cuttings are vegetative propagation and have a different starting point from sowing seeds to raise seedlings.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-propagation-p2: A plant raised from seed is called a seedling. The source uses seed propagation for raising rootstocks and breeding new cultivars. Remember these purposes separately from multiplying nursery plants of the cultivar intended for harvest.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-propagation-p3: The rootstock forming the base of a graft is selected from varieties with good root development and disease resistance. Resistance does not mean complete immunity to every pest or disease; the condition of the nursery plant itself must also be checked.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-propagation-p4: A superior cultivar that produces good fruit is used for the scion joined to the rootstock. Select scions free of pest and disease damage as well. Do not confuse the rootstock’s role with the scion’s role in determining the harvested fruit.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-propagation-p5: Cuttings are plant parts removed and inserted into soil or growing medium to produce shoots and roots. Grapes and figs are examples in the source. Distinguish this from sowing seeds and germinating them.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-propagation-p6: In layering, a branch roots while still attached to the parent and is separated after roots develop. The source shows bending part of a branch into soil and removing bark from part of a branch to encourage rooting. The key difference from cuttings is that a cutting is separated first.

agr-fruit-foundation-propagation.activity: For grafting, cuttings, layering and seed propagation, organize the materials used and the time of separation from the parent. Explain the properties sought in rootstocks and scions separately too.

agr-fruit-foundation-graft-types.title: Branch grafting and budding
agr-fruit-foundation-graft-types.objective: Distinguish basic graft types by the material joined and the way it connects to the rootstock.

paragraphTitles.agr-fruit-foundation-graft-types-p3: The key point in cut grafting
paragraphTitles.agr-fruit-foundation-graft-types-p4: The key point in cleft grafting
paragraphTitles.agr-fruit-foundation-graft-types-p5: The key point in side grafting

paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-graft-types-p1: Grafting produces a nursery tree by joining a scion to a rootstock. The source lists purposes including multiplying the same cultivar or line, bringing forward the start of fruit bearing and using resistant rootstocks.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-graft-types-p2: Joining a piece of branch is branch grafting; joining a bud is budding. Beyond memorizing names, check whether a branch or a bud is transferred to the rootstock to explain differences in the diagrams.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-graft-types-p3: The cut-grafting diagram shows inserting the scion where its cambium aligns with the rootstock’s cambium. Merely bringing the two materials into contact is not the point: identify the tissue that must align.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-graft-types-p4: Cleft grafting inserts a wedge-shaped scion into a split in the rootstock. The source shows its use in renewing main branches. Compare the insertion position with side grafting, which joins a scion partway along a stock.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-graft-types-p5: The side-grafting diagram shows joining a scion partway along a branch or trunk without cutting that branch or trunk off. To distinguish it from types that first sever the stock, look at the joining position and whether the original branch remains.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-graft-types-p6: Budding includes T-budding and chip budding. In the T-shaped example, a bud is inserted into a cut in the rootstock and taped while the bud remains exposed. Differences in names do not mean that every bud may be covered over.

agr-fruit-foundation-graft-types.activity: Describe the material joined and its position on the stock in one sentence each for cut grafting, cleft grafting, side grafting and budding. Also identify points that require separate practical learning with diagrams.

agr-fruit-foundation-graft-alignment.title: Graft alignment and planting position
agr-fruit-foundation-graft-alignment.objective: Explain cambium alignment and planting with the graft union above ground.

paragraphTitles.agr-fruit-foundation-graft-alignment-p3: A guide to tissue that is difficult to see
paragraphTitles.agr-fruit-foundation-graft-alignment-p5: Preventing the cut surfaces from drying

paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-graft-alignment-p1: In a branch cross-section, the cambium lies between the phloem toward the bark and the xylem toward the inside. This is the part to align in grafting. Matching only the cut outlines or the branch centers does not necessarily align the intended tissue.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-graft-alignment-p2: Rootstock and scion may differ in thickness. The source’s cross-section illustrates placing the scion to one side so their cambia meet. A thin scion should not simply be placed in the center of a thick stock.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-graft-alignment-p3: The cambium is difficult to confirm with the naked eye, so the diagram uses the outside of the xylem as a positional guide. Link the names of the tissues in cross-section with the idea of where to make the actual join.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-graft-alignment-p4: The source shows taping the grafted materials so they do not separate. Avoiding a gap between stock and scion and maintaining their alignment are the diagram’s key points. The appearance of secure binding alone does not prove tissue alignment.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-graft-alignment-p5: The source indicates preventing cut surfaces from drying during grafting. The post-grafting diagrams show grafting wax on the stock’s cut surface and covering with a polyethylene bag. Learn the illustrated sequence without independently adding material quantities or removal times.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-graft-alignment-p6: The planting diagram for a grafted nursery tree shows the rootstock–scion union above ground. Putting roots in soil is not the same as burying the union deeply too. Identify the grafted part of the plant before planting.

agr-fruit-foundation-graft-alignment.activity: Using a rootstock and scion of different thicknesses as an example, explain why the cambium position matters rather than their centers. Also indicate where the graft union should be after planting.

agr-fruit-foundation-pruning.title: Pruning purposes and two ways of cutting
agr-fruit-foundation-pruning.objective: Connect pruning severity and the difference between heading-back and thinning cuts with branch growth and arrangement.

paragraphTitles.agr-fruit-foundation-pruning-p6: Look at the whole tree before cutting

paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-pruning-p1: Training creates tree form and branch arrangement by cutting branches or adjusting their direction. Pruning is the cutting of branches and supports stable harvests of good fruit and trees that are easier to work on.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-pruning-p2: Heavy pruning tends to stimulate vegetative growth. Light pruning is described as tending to restrain vegetative growth and encourage reproductive growth. Cutting more does not necessarily produce more flowers or fruit.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-pruning-p3: Fruit-tree pruning is mainly winter work, with summer pruning shown as supplementary. Do not select branches to cut by the season’s name alone; check the species and which branches bear fruit.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-pruning-p4: Heading back shortens an extended branch by cutting partway along it. For a slender branch being retained, the source shows cutting above a leaf bud facing the desired direction of growth. Explain that part of the branch remains.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-pruning-p5: Thinning removes an unwanted branch at its base. Unlike shortening a branch partway along it, this reduces crowding and aims for an arrangement admitting air and light. The diagrams also show different tools for thick and thin branches.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-pruning-p6: First examine the whole tree: the arrangement of main and secondary scaffold branches, crowding and fruit-bearing positions. The illustrated sequence starts with the main branches and examines from tip toward base. Do not cut every branch uniformly after looking at just one bud.

agr-fruit-foundation-pruning.activity: Draw the difference between shortening the same branch partway along it and removing it at its base, and label the two operations. List three things to examine on the whole tree before cutting.

agr-fruit-foundation-treeforms.title: Recognizing tree forms and branch training
agr-fruit-foundation-treeforms.objective: Distinguish tree forms by the arrangement of the central trunk and main branches, and explain training that adjusts young branches’ direction.

paragraphTitles.agr-fruit-foundation-treeforms-p1: Look at trunk and branch arrangement

paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-treeforms-p1: When examining tree form, consider the central trunk and the main branches extending from it, not just tree height. Training varies with species and cultivar, so do not prescribe one form even for the same kind of fruit tree.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-treeforms-p2: The central-leader diagram arranges branches around a clearly retained central trunk. Dwarf apple and peach cultivation are given as examples. This does not mean that every apple or peach must always be trained in this form.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-treeforms-p3: The modified central-leader form has a different trunk and scaffold arrangement from the central-leader form; persimmons are among the source’s examples. Do not identify it by branch number alone: check the trunk’s continuation and where the main branches arise.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-treeforms-p4: The natural open-center diagram arranges branches to leave the upper center of the tree open. Both sources give examples including peaches, plums and Japanese apricots. Explain its difference from a diagram retaining a clearly defined central trunk.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-treeforms-p5: Overhead trellis training spreads branches horizontally over a support framework. Grapes and pears are main examples. A low drawing alone does not establish trellis training; check the relationship between the support and branches.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-treeforms-p6: In pears and grapes, branch training adjusts the direction in which young branches grow. Distinguishing this work from pruning, which shortens branches by cutting, makes their different roles in forming the tree easier to explain.

agr-fruit-foundation-treeforms.activity: Explain the four tree forms using the terms central trunk, main branch and support framework. Also describe how directing a young grape branch differs from pruning.

agr-fruit-foundation-pollination.title: From pollination to fruit development
agr-fruit-foundation-pollination.objective: Distinguish pollination, fertilization and parthenocarpy, and explain the sequence of changes in fruit cell number and cell size.

paragraphTitles.agr-fruit-foundation-pollination-p2: Pollination and fertilization are different terms
paragraphTitles.agr-fruit-foundation-pollination-p3: The role of a pollen-source tree

paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-pollination-p1: Pollination places pollen on the pistil when a flower opens. Fruit-bearing management includes artificial pollination by people and use of insects such as bees. The fact that a flower has opened does not show that pollination is complete.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-pollination-p2: The usual explanation proceeds from pollination to fertilization and then fruit set. Treat pollen reaching the pistil and the subsequent fertilization as separate stages. This distinction is also necessary for understanding parthenocarpy.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-pollination-p3: The source shows planting trees of another cultivar to help fruit set. Preparing artificial-pollination tools and providing trees that supply pollen have different roles. Do not assume that all cultivar combinations work equally well.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-pollination-p4: Development of fruit without fertilization is called parthenocarpy. Examples include Satsuma mandarins, figs and the persimmon cultivar Hiratanenashi. Do not confuse it with fertilization by a flower’s own pollen or fruit development without flowers.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-pollination-p5: Fruit development is explained as an initial increase in cell number followed by enlargement of the cells. Do not treat seeing a large fruit as identical to the stage when cell number increases.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-pollination-p6: As maturation progresses, sugars accumulate and most fruits become sweeter. Cellular changes also soften fruit. Preserve the scope of “most” rather than saying that every fruit reaches the same sweetness or firmness.

agr-fruit-foundation-pollination.activity: Explain pollination, fertilization and parthenocarpy separately. Arrange fruit development into the stage of increasing cell number and the stage of increasing cell size.

agr-fruit-foundation-definition-2.title: Multi-year growth and fruit-crop classification
agr-fruit-foundation-definition-2.objective: Read the Level 2 definition through growing duration and plant characteristics, distinguishing it from everyday fruit names and statistical indicators.

paragraphTitles.agr-fruit-foundation-definition-2-p2: Different from crops that die within a year
paragraphTitles.agr-fruit-foundation-definition-2-p4: Do not overlook woody and herbaceous plants

paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-definition-2-p1: Level 2 includes woody and herbaceous plants grown for at least 2 years to harvest their fruit in its definition of fruit crops. Do not narrow the definition to woody plants just because the Japanese term contains the character for tree; check duration and harvest purpose together.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-definition-2-p2: Melons and watermelons also produce fruit for harvest, but the source treats them as vegetables because they are herbaceous plants that die within one year. Do not classify fruit crops and vegetables solely by whether the harvested part is a fruit.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-definition-2-p3: Chestnuts and Japanese apricots illustrate differences between everyday treatment as fruit and classification in cultivation. They are studied as fruit crops because fruit is harvested from trees that grow over multiple years. Do not change categories based only on taste or use as food.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-definition-2-p4: This definition combines whether a plant is woody or herbaceous with how many years it is grown. Shortening it to “only multi-year woody plants” or “all herbs producing fruit” changes the source’s scope.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-definition-2-p5: In the Level 2 source’s 2021 example, Satsuma mandarins, apples and pears are listed among crops with large harvest quantities, while grapes, apples and Satsuma mandarins are listed for high production value. Separate quantity indicators from monetary indicators, and do not replace a historical year’s information with current rankings.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-definition-2-p6: When grouping crops, check growing duration, whether they are woody or herbaceous, and the purpose of harvesting fruit. Be able to explain everyday culinary or shop names separately from classification criteria used in cultivation studies.

agr-fruit-foundation-definition-2.activity: Explain the source’s categories for melons and chestnuts using growing duration and plant characteristics. Always include the reference year when giving examples of harvest quantity and production value.

agr-fruit-foundation-bud-patterns-2.title: Pure flower buds, mixed buds and fruit-bearing branches
agr-fruit-foundation-bud-patterns-2.objective: Read the Level 2 bud categories and three branch diagrams, distinguishing flower position from branch changes since the previous year.

paragraphTitles.agr-fruit-foundation-bud-patterns-2-p1: Leaves only, flowers only, or both
paragraphTitles.agr-fruit-foundation-bud-patterns-2-p3: The pattern bearing directly on last year’s branch
paragraphTitles.agr-fruit-foundation-bud-patterns-2-p4: The pattern at tips of fruiting branches
paragraphTitles.agr-fruit-foundation-bud-patterns-2-p5: The pattern in leaf axils of new shoots

paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-bud-patterns-2-p1: Level 2 distinguishes leaf buds producing leaves, pure flower buds producing flowers only, and mixed buds producing leaves and flowers. The first point is not to reinterpret all flower buds as buds producing only flowers.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-bud-patterns-2-p2: The branch diagrams use separate symbols for leaf buds, pure or mixed flower buds, and fruit or fruit clusters. Do not count every round symbol as a bud; check the legend to establish what each symbol represents.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-bud-patterns-2-p3: In the first pattern, flower buds on branches grown the previous year open and become fruit at that location. Peaches, plums, Japanese apricots, cherries and apricots are examples. Continue following their relationship with the branches remaining the following year.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-bud-patterns-2-p4: In the second pattern, the tip or upper axillary buds of a fruiting branch formed the previous year extend slightly, and flower buds at their ends open. Apples, pears and blueberries are examples. Do not see the previous year’s branch and the part extended during flowering merely as one unchanged-length branch.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-bud-patterns-2-p5: In the third pattern, flower buds arise in the leaf axils of the current year’s new shoots and then flower and bear fruit. Grapes, kiwifruit, persimmons and chestnuts are illustrated. Also identify the junction between a leaf and its branch.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-foundation-bud-patterns-2-p6: Placing the diagrams for the first, second and third years in sequence distinguishes the flower-bearing part from the part later retained as a branch. Because flower positions differ, do not transfer a pruning diagram unchanged to fruit trees with another pattern.

agr-fruit-foundation-bud-patterns-2.activity: For the three patterns, describe the previous year’s branch, the current year’s new shoot and flower-bud location. Explain pure and mixed flower buds without confusing them with the round fruit symbols.

agr-fruit-manage-bagging.title: Comparing bagging of peaches and grape clusters
agr-fruit-manage-bagging.objective: Explain the purposes of bagging and distinguish crop-specific positioning and precautions when fastening the bag.

paragraphTitles.agr-fruit-manage-bagging-p6: Do not damage the fastening point

paragraphs.agr-fruit-manage-bagging-p1: Bagging protects fruit against pest and disease damage and helps produce a clean appearance. It acts on the crop differently from fruit thinning, which removes fruit.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-manage-bagging-p2: The source shows separate bags for peaches and grapes. Match the crop name to the bag shape rather than assuming that every bag’s opening attaches at the same place.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-manage-bagging-p3: In the peach example, the bag is opened, the branch passes through its slit, and the fruit is placed centrally inside. Check the fruit’s position, not only the bag opening.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-manage-bagging-p4: In the peach example, gather the opening on the opposite side of the branch, fold the fastener toward the branch base and wrap it around the branch. Distinguish this from fastening to the grape cluster stalk.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-manage-bagging-p5: For grapes, place the cluster centrally in the open bag. The illustrated example gathers the side without a fastener first, then the fastener side, and closes the opening by folding the fastener and wrapping it around the cluster stalk.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-manage-bagging-p6: Both examples place fruit centrally in the bag. The fastener must not crush the fruit stalk or branch when wrapped around it. Tightening the opening as firmly as possible is not the only standard of good work.

agr-fruit-manage-bagging.activity: For peaches and grapes, make three columns: what goes in the bag, where the opening is gathered and which parts must not be damaged. Explain an off-center fruit and a fastener crushing its stalk as separate problems.

agr-fruit-manage-harvest.title: Harvest maturity and cutting Satsuma mandarins
agr-fruit-manage-harvest.objective: Distinguish ripening on the tree from ripening after harvest and explain the two-cut sequence for Satsuma mandarins.

paragraphTitles.agr-fruit-manage-harvest-p5: Separating a mandarin from its branch

paragraphs.agr-fruit-manage-harvest-p1: The time fruit is removed from a tree does not necessarily coincide with the time it is ready to eat. For each fruit species, distinguish waiting for ripening on the tree from allowing ripening after harvest.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-manage-harvest-p2: Both sources list apples, Japanese pears and citrus as examples harvested after they mature. Even though both are called pears, do not transfer the explanation of European pears directly to Japanese pears.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-manage-harvest-p3: European pears and kiwifruit illustrate postharvest ripening during storage. This is different from the idea that every fruit should be harvested as early and immature as possible.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-manage-harvest-p4: The source gives ranges such as late June to late August for peaches. Read the crop and the span of the season instead of taking one calendar day as a nationwide harvest date.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-manage-harvest-p5: In the Satsuma example, cut the fruit free from its branch without injuring it with the scissor tips. Pulling fruit off can damage it, so distinguish cutting from pulling.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-manage-harvest-p6: After separating the fruit from the branch, the example shows cutting the long portion of the remaining fruit stalk a second time. Two-cut harvesting does not mean that the blade may contact the fruit during the first cut.

agr-fruit-manage-harvest.activity: Group apples, Japanese pears, European pears and kiwifruit into examples that wait for maturity and examples that ripen after harvest. Then explain the sequence and precautions for separating a mandarin from its branch and trimming the remaining stalk.

agr-fruit-manage-renewal.title: Renewing cultivars through replanting and topworking
agr-fruit-manage-renewal.objective: Distinguish replacing trees with new nursery plants from grafting onto existing branches, and read the two patterns of topworking.

paragraphTitles.agr-fruit-manage-renewal-p1: The task of renewing an orchard
paragraphTitles.agr-fruit-manage-renewal-p2: Replanting replaces trees with nursery plants
paragraphTitles.agr-fruit-manage-renewal-p4: A pattern cutting the original branch
paragraphTitles.agr-fruit-manage-renewal-p5: A pattern retaining a support branch
paragraphTitles.agr-fruit-manage-renewal-p6: Separate explaining a method from carrying it out

paragraphs.agr-fruit-manage-renewal-p1: In long-established fruit trees, declining vigor and reduced yields may become problems. The source discusses methods of renewing cultivars in orchards with old trees or unsuitable cultivars.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-manage-renewal-p2: Replanting uses new nursery trees. It renews a different target from grafting a new branch onto the existing tree. Check whether new plants or existing trees are being used.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-manage-renewal-p3: Topworking grafts branches of another cultivar onto the existing fruit tree’s branches. The diagrams show graft positions partway along main or secondary scaffold branches; it is not simply planting a new nursery tree nearby.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-manage-renewal-p4: One topworking diagram shows the original branch being cut. The graft position and the point at which the original branch is cut are marked differently; distinguish arrows from the scion symbols.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-manage-renewal-p5: The other pattern retains the original branch as a supporting branch. The name topworking alone does not mean that every original branch is cut off. Recognize that the source shows two patterns.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-manage-renewal-p6: When communicating orchard-renewal methods, identify replanting versus topworking, and for topworking identify how the original branch is handled. This schematic alone cannot determine the cut position or grafting time suitable for an actual tree.

agr-fruit-manage-renewal.activity: Explain separately a proposal using new nursery trees and one grafting onto existing branches. Compare the two topworking patterns, organizing whether the original branch is cut or retained and which practical checks cannot be decided from the schematic.

agr-fruit-manage-orchard-soil.title: Protecting the orchard surface and managing water
agr-fruit-manage-orchard-soil.objective: Compare surface management on slopes and explain the root environment by considering both water retention and drainage.

paragraphs.agr-fruit-manage-orchard-soil-p1: Rain-driven soil erosion is a problem in sloping orchards. When comparing management that keeps the ground vegetation-free, consider that surface soil becomes more easily washed away.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-manage-orchard-soil-p2: Methods include laying rice straw or cut grass over the surface and growing grass to cover it. Do not combine bare ground, laid mulch and living grass cover as though they were the same management method.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-manage-orchard-soil-p3: The source also describes combining several surface-management approaches. Rather than evaluating the whole orchard by one overall appearance, be able to explain which areas are covered by which method.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-manage-orchard-soil-p4: Drainage ditches that reduce soil wash-off and stone walls that help prevent collapse are listed. Covering the ground and providing drainage or soil-support structures have different roles.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-manage-orchard-soil-p5: Deep cultivation and adding organic matter are explained in connection with improved water retention and aeration. Suitable soil pH also varies by fruit species, so do not assume that every species requires the same adjustment.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-manage-orchard-soil-p6: Consider irrigation timing and quantity according to fruit species and growth condition. Soil needs not only to retain water but also to drain excess water. Increasing irrigation alone does not constitute improving the root environment.

agr-fruit-manage-orchard-soil.activity: Imagine a sloping orchard and distinguish bare ground, laid grass mulch and areas with growing grass. Separately explain erosion control, drainage and the conditions of water and air around roots.

agr-fruit-manage-fertilizer.title: Reading fruit-tree basal and supplementary fertilizers by role
agr-fruit-manage-fertilizer.objective: Explain fruit-tree fertilization by role, timing and application position, distinguishing spring, summer and autumn supplementary applications.

paragraphTitles.agr-fruit-manage-fertilizer-p1: The annual foundation and supplementary supply
paragraphTitles.agr-fruit-manage-fertilizer-p4: Spring fertilizer for buds, branches and leaves
paragraphTitles.agr-fruit-manage-fertilizer-p6: Autumn fertilizer for vigor and stored nutrients

paragraphs.agr-fruit-manage-fertilizer-p1: Basal fertilizer provides the nutrient foundation for a fruit tree’s annual growth, while supplementary fertilizer makes up what basal fertilizer alone does not supply. These are not merely different names for applications with the same purpose.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-manage-fertilizer-p2: The source gives the dormant period before growth begins as the time for basal fertilizer, with December–January for deciduous fruit trees and March–April for evergreens as examples. Do not convert this into an instruction to fertilize on the same date in every region.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-manage-fertilizer-p3: For mature trees, surface application to the soil is described. Other methods include incorporating fertilizer through the soil profile with organic matter during deep cultivation, and foliar spraying of nutrients dissolved in water over the entire tree.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-manage-fertilizer-p4: Spring fertilizer is supplementary feeding to support new buds, branches and leaves; it is also called bud-emergence fertilizer. Distinguish it from summer fertilizer intended to support fruit growth.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-manage-fertilizer-p5: Summer fertilizer supports fruit development and is also called fruit fertilizer. The source’s distinction between spring, summer and autumn relates to purposes, not simply memorizing season names.
paragraphs.agr-fruit-manage-fertilizer-p6: Autumn fertilizer is supplementary feeding to restore vigor and increase stored nutrients; it is also called postharvest “thank-you” fertilizer. The source explains using quick-acting fertilizers for spring, summer and autumn supplementary feeding.
